text:
Why do people always try to run these cards at resolutions beyond their limits? Never makes sense to me. 1080p is a horrible choice of resolution for this card. 1440p is just flat out dumb.

Guys... Look.

This is a 1280x720 card. There is nothing wrong with 720p. 720p is a resolution, that's it. It doesn't make your games look better or worse. It's just a pixel grid the card uses to map pixels on your screen.

BUT EXILE 720p LOOKS DOG WATER! WHY WOULD I USE THAT! UGH!

No. 720p looks bad on CERTAIN! displays. For 720p, you want to use a 1440p monitor...

Why? YOU SAID ITS 720P!? WHY WOULD YOU USE THIS ON A 1440P monitor!? YOUR DUMB EXILE.

No, I am not. You want to use a 1440p monitor and 1280x720 as your resolution of choice for the following reasons...

1. This card uses a 64 bit memory bus and has limited 4 GB of GDDR6. You are heavily memory bandwidth limited. So to get the most out of this card, you need to make that memory go further. How do you do this? Use a lower resolution to reduce the memory footprint and memory transfer sizes; 720p textures are a lot smaller than 1080p, 1440p, and 4k textures. So, 720p resolution is a good place to be. You don't want to use XeSS either because you just don't have enough memory to reliably use this feature; So, don't even bother using XeSS, turning this on only hurts performance regardless of whatever numbers you might be seeing. You are eating up frametime budget that you just don't have on a card like this.

2. 720p is a 2x integer scale on a 1440p pixel grid.

2560x1440 = 1440p.
1280x720 = 720p.

2560/2 = 1280
1440/2 = 720

Because it's an integer scale, it will look clean and crisp on the 1440p monitor, not blurry or horrible which most people associate when 720p. They usually try doing this on a 4k display or 1080p display, and yeah on those display grids, it will look horrible, but it's not because of the resolution. The reason 720p looks bad on a 1080p display is the scaling factor isn't integer based, it's floating. You don't want a floating point scale for your image, you want an integer scale, 1:1, 2:1, 3:1, etc. If you want it to look even better, use a smaller size screen that supports a 1440p pixel grid natively. PPI makes a difference in how image clarity is perceived. PPI is directly relational to screen native resolution, resolution being used, and over all screen size.

The standard PPI value most people associate with a native 1440p panel is 108.79+ PPI, so a mini 1440p 13" display is the ideal screen size to achieve 1440p clarity with a 720p resolution. They do sell displays at this size that are quite good and many have VESA mounting capabilities you can use to create a custom monitor stand to mount these small screens.

1280 x 720 (720p)
@27" = 54.39 PPI
@ 17" = 86.39 PPI
@ 15.6" = 94.14 PPI
@ 14" = 104.90 PPI 
@ 13.3" = 110.24 PPI

But Exile, the PPI is so bad at 27" It will look terrible! NO! Because it's a perfect integer scale! Integer scale is what matters when scaling a resolution to a monitor for clarity. So while PPI is noticeably down, it's still perfectly half that of 1440p on a 27" display.

108.79 PPI / 2 = 54.39 PPI

You might notice a bit of chucky pixels with no AA and depending on the game, but that can be alleviated using some AA or post processing AA options the games tend to offer. The trade off is worth it.

3. Using lower resolutions allows you to turn up settings with minimal performance losses. You have some more memory available so you can turn things up. Just be reasonable with what settings you are adjusting. You definitely aren't going to be using AA at x8 on a card like this, even at 720p resolution, but 2x/4x? Maybe. Depends on the type of AA being utilized and the game in question.

What if I want to use a 1080p screen?

Use half of 1080p's resolution to reduce the load and memory footprint. It won't look great though, once you go below 720p, you lose quite a bit of detail. You are no longer in High Def territory, but in Standard Definition ranges so things just won't look as good on a modern display.

1920 /2 = 960
1080 /2 = 540

But again, I don't recommend this on a modern pixel grid display because you exit the Hif Def range. You need a certain amount of pixels on your pixel grid otherwise you get to muddy.

However, if you have yourself a CRT display, this could actually work out quite nicely and you would gain even more performance. So it just depends on what you are trying to use it with.

Hope this helps everyone. Cheers!

text: I should also state the the GPU is a power efficient GPU. It's frame rate target is 30-40 fps. Not 60, not 120, etc. Now can it hit those higher frame rates and the like? Probably, depending on the game and settings used, but don't expect it. Expect 30-40 fps. You should also CAP your FPS using a tool like RivaTuner to improve performance stability and reduce power draw, which is what this card is mainly designed around, power limited and power conscience scenarios. The card also has an AV1 encoder, if I am not mistaken, so that makes it an excellent GPU for video editing and streaming. Remember though, your system will need 32GB or more of Memory to really see the benefits of this in that type of workload.

text: @RyzesTechZone  You are correct. It is entirely depending on BIOS and motherboard. You will want REBAR for these Intel cards and there is no way around it. You just lose way to much performance otherwise and there is no getting around that limitation. That is a design choice of these modern Intel ARC cards. As it is they are very bad with DX9, DX10, and DX11 since they don't have hardware to handle these direct X versions natively so they are emulated in the driver stack. This is why you need pretty beefy CPUs to get the true performance these cards have on offer. Intel's driver stack has massive overhead issues due to the emulation of those older versions of DX. These ARC cards are mainly Vulkan and DX12 cards and if your game has options to use DX12/Vulkan, you should 100% opt to use them.
author: @theexile4694

text: Re-BAR is part of the PCIe spec and it technically supported on ALL systems with PCIe Gen3 and some Gen2. The issue is that there needs to be a BIOS that adds in the options to enable Re-BAR and Above 4G Decoding. The vast majority of board manufacturers did not bother doing this and none of the OEM systems did. If the system is older than 10th Gen Intel, just assume it's not going to be there. AM4 is a different animal thanks to AMDs willingness to support newer CPUs. So, you probably have BIOS updates that add the option in for early AM4 boards.
